title: The Bases of Social Power
publication: In D. Cartwright (Ed.), Studies in Social Power (pp. 150–167). Ann Arbor: Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, editor, volume title, 1959 date, Ann Arbor publication and pages 150–167 matched on the Institute for Social Research site (cdn.isr.umich.edu), which hosts a digitized copy of the chapter and of the full volume; bibbase.org lists the same pages. Sources disagree on whether the publisher is styled the University of Michigan Press; the ISR copy was followed.

summary: French and Raven proposed that the power one person holds over another rests on a small number of distinct bases: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert power. Each base is defined from the perspective of the person being influenced: power exists because the target believes the agent can reward, punish, rightfully direct, serve as a model of identification, or knows more. The chapter is a theoretical typology, not an empirical study.
arguments: Power is a relation between an agent and a target, located in the target’s perceptions, not a possession of the agent alone.
Five bases are distinguished: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert.
Different bases have different side effects; coercion, for example, requires surveillance and tends to reduce attraction to the agent.
The range of a base differs: expert power, for instance, is limited to the domain in which the agent is seen as knowledgeable.
design: Conceptual typology drawing on the authors’ field theory tradition; no new data.
strengths: Simple, memorable and still the most widely used vocabulary for the sources of interpersonal power; defined from the target’s perspective, which keeps attention on perception.
limitations: The bases overlap (a boss’s legitimate power usually carries reward and coercive power with it); the typology is about interpersonal power and says little about structural sources such as control of resources or network position; later research measuring the bases has relied heavily on self-report questionnaires.
contested: Not contested as a vocabulary; its usefulness as a measurement framework is debated. Raven later added informational power as a further base. Structural accounts of power (R-pfeffer-1978-external) treat the bases as consequences of dependence rather than as primary.
generalizability: Transfers well as a diagnostic vocabulary for any organization, including sports organizations. It does not predict which base will work in a given setting.
relevance: Gives you the language to separate the authority your title grants from the power that colleagues actually attribute to you.

title: The External Control of Organizations: A Resource Dependence Perspective
publication: Original edition 1978; reissued as a Stanford Business Classic by Stanford University Press, 2003 (with a new preface by Pfeffer)
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors and the 2003 Stanford University Press reissue (Stanford Business Classics, new preface by Pfeffer) matched on gsb.stanford.edu and sup.org; a 1978 original date appeared in a listing but the original publisher was not confirmed in search results, so it is not named here.

summary: Pfeffer and Salancik argue that organizations are best understood through their dependence on external actors who control resources they need. Because dependence creates the possibility of external control, much of what organizations do — co-opting outsiders onto boards, forming alliances, merging, diversifying suppliers — can be read as attempts to manage dependence. The same logic, building on power-dependence theory in sociology, explains power inside organizations: units that supply what others critically need, and cannot easily get elsewhere, gain influence.
arguments: An organization’s dependence on another actor grows with the importance of the resource, the other actor’s discretion over it, and the scarcity of alternatives.
Dependence creates the possibility of external control; organizations respond by managing or restructuring their dependencies.
Common responses include co-optation, alliances, mergers and diversification of resource sources.
Power is relational and situational: it shifts when critical contingencies shift.
design: Theoretical book synthesizing prior empirical work; tested extensively by later studies.
strengths: One of the foundational theories of organizations; turns power from a personality trait into a structural relation that can be mapped and changed.
limitations: Explains why actors gain influence better than how they use it; later reviews note that the theory was often invoked as a metaphor rather than tested directly.
contested: Broadly accepted as a perspective; individual predictions (for example about mergers or board co-optation) have mixed support. Institutional theory (R-dimaggio-1983-iron) offers a competing explanation of the same organizational behavior.
generalizability: High for any organization that depends on outside resources — public agencies, hospitals, firms and sports organizations alike.
relevance: The clearest way to answer “who actually has leverage here, and why?” before you try to change anything.

title: Managing with Power: Politics and Influence in Organizations
publication: Boston: Harvard Business School Press (hardcover 1992; paperback 1994)
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (Harvard Business School Press) and 1992 hardcover date matched in the publisher-derived copyright page on an O’Reilly listing and in library catalogs (NYPL, folio.caval.edu.au); Google Books listing found.

summary: A book for managers arguing that getting things done in organizations requires understanding and using power, and that discomfort with power leads capable people to fail at implementation. Pfeffer synthesizes research on the sources of power, including structural position and control of resources, together with extended organizational examples, and discusses the strategies and tactics through which power is used.
arguments: Implementation problems are largely problems of influence: mobilizing support and overcoming resistance.
Power comes substantially from structural position, control of resources and information, and alliances, not only from personal attributes.
Timing, framing and the management of interpersonal relations are tools for using power.
Managers who avoid power out of discomfort tend to lose to those who do not.
design: Practitioner synthesis by an organizational scholar; illustrative cases and narrative review, not a new empirical test.
strengths: Grounded in the author’s own academic research tradition; unsentimental about how organizations work; useful catalog of sources and tactics.
limitations: Case-based illustration is vulnerable to selection (vivid successes are chosen); prescriptive claims are not tested as such; limited treatment of the costs of political behavior for trust and for others.
contested: The normative stance — that managers should actively build and use power — is contested on ethical and practical grounds; see the influence ethics discussion and R-yukl-1992-consequences on which tactics build commitment.
generalizability: Written about large U.S. organizations; the structural insights transfer widely, the tactical advice depends on culture and context.
relevance: A deliberately uncomfortable counterweight to the belief that good analysis will be adopted on its merits.

title: The Strength of Weak Ties
license: © The University of Chicago. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 78, issue 6, pages 1360–1380 and DOI 10.1086/225469 matched in a BibSonomy record and Wikipedia’s reference list; JSTOR stable URL also reported. Copies circulate on university course pages; library access recommended.

summary: Granovetter argues that weak ties — acquaintances rather than close friends — are disproportionately important for moving information and opportunity across social groups, because strong ties tend to connect people who already know each other and share the same information. He links this micro-level property of ties to macro outcomes such as diffusion, mobility and community organization, and supports it with evidence from a study of how professional, technical and managerial workers found jobs.
arguments: Strongly tied people tend to share contacts, so their information is redundant; bridges between groups are almost always weak ties.
Weak ties therefore carry novel information and opportunities across social boundaries.
In the job-search data, people who found jobs through contacts had more often seen those contacts only occasionally or rarely than often.
Communities with few weak ties may struggle to organize collectively.
design: Theoretical argument illustrated with data from the author’s survey of people who had recently changed jobs; descriptive, not causal.
strengths: Elegant mechanism linking network structure to outcomes; one of the most cited papers in social science; generated decades of testable predictions.
limitations: Original evidence is descriptive and limited to one labor market; tie strength was measured crudely by frequency of contact; cannot separate the effect of ties from the characteristics of people who have them.
contested: Core claim has been refined rather than overturned: a large randomized test (R-rajkumar-2022-causal) found that moderately weak ties, not the weakest, were most helpful for job mobility.
generalizability: Strong for information flow in labor markets and organizations; the importance of weak versus strong ties varies by industry and by what is being transmitted (information versus trust or support).
relevance: Explains why the colleague you rarely talk to in another department may be your best source of new information and your best route for spreading a change.

title: Structural Holes and Good Ideas
license: © The University of Chicago. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 110, issue 2, pages 349–399 and DOI 10.1086/421787 matched in search results (doi listing, Stanford SNAP course reading copy, scilit.com).

summary: Burt argues that people whose networks span structural holes — gaps between groups that are not otherwise connected — are more likely to have good ideas, because they see combinations of perspectives that people inside one group do not. Using data on supply-chain managers in a large American electronics company, he reports that managers whose networks spanned holes were more likely to voice ideas, less likely to have them dismissed and more likely to have them judged valuable, and also received more favorable evaluations, compensation and promotion.
arguments: Opinion and behavior are more homogeneous within groups than between them, so brokers across groups see alternatives earlier.
Brokerage across structural holes is associated with ideas that senior managers rate as valuable.
Brokerage is also associated with compensation, positive performance evaluations and promotion.
The value of a good idea depends on being able to move it across groups, not only on generating it.
design: Network survey of managers in one company linked to ideas they proposed (rated by senior managers) and to career outcomes; cross-sectional association.
strengths: Direct measurement of network structure; outcome measures independent of the respondent (ideas rated by others, compensation records); clear mechanism.
limitations: Single firm; observational design cannot rule out that able or ambitious people build brokerage networks (reverse causation); brokerage may carry costs, such as distrust, that the design does not capture.
contested: The benefits of brokerage versus closure (dense, trusting networks) remain debated, and appear to depend on culture and task; see R-granovetter-1973-strength for the related weak-ties argument.
generalizability: Plausible in knowledge work where combining perspectives matters; less certain in settings that reward loyalty and closure.
relevance: Bridging groups — for example across departments, languages or countries — is a structural asset, and also a responsibility.

title: A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ties

verified.evidence: Title, five authors, journal, volume 377, issue 6612, pages 1304–1310 and DOI 10.1126/science.abl4476 matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab publication page; an author copy is posted on ide.mit.edu.

summary: Using multiple large-scale randomized experiments on LinkedIn’s “People You May Know” recommendation feature, which varied the kinds of connections offered to more than 20 million members, the authors provide a causal test of Granovetter’s weak-ties hypothesis for job mobility. They find an inverted-U relationship: moderately weak ties were most associated with job transmission, while the weakest and strongest ties were less helpful, and weak ties mattered more in more digital industries.
arguments: Experimental variation in network formation allows a causal estimate of the value of weak ties, which earlier observational work could not provide.
The relationship between tie strength and job mobility is nonlinear (inverted U), not “the weaker the better”.
The value of weak versus strong ties differs across industries.
design: Randomized experiments embedded in a platform’s connection-recommendation algorithm, analysed for downstream job transitions.
strengths: Very large scale; randomization addresses the selection problem that weakens most network studies; directly tests a classic theory.
limitations: One platform and one outcome (job mobility); tie strength is measured by structural proxies on an online network; raised public discussion about experimentation on platform users.
contested: Supports and refines R-granovetter-1973-strength rather than contradicting it.
generalizability: Strong for information-driven labor markets; inferences to influence inside a single organization are by analogy.
relevance: A model of how a famous idea can be tested causally — and of how the tested version turns out more nuanced than the slogan.

title: Informal Networks: The Company Behind the Chart
license: © Harvard Business School Publishing. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, the July–August 1993 issue of Harvard Business Review and pages 104–111 matched in several search results (bookshare.org, a university executive-education reading list, a Sage reprint page in an edited volume); the hbr.org page did not appear in results, so the Sage reprint page is linked.

summary: Krackhardt and Hanson argue that much of an organization’s real work runs through informal networks that the formal chart does not show, and that managers can map them with simple questionnaires. They distinguish advice networks (who depends on whom for technical help), trust networks (who shares sensitive information) and communication networks (who talks about work regularly), and describe recurring problem patterns such as a single person bridging otherwise separate groups.
arguments: The formal chart shows authority; informal networks show how work, advice and trust actually flow.
Advice, trust and communication networks differ and answer different managerial questions.
Network maps can be drawn from short surveys and cross-checked against managers’ assumptions.
Structural patterns — isolated groups, gaps, over-reliance on one connector — signal predictable problems.
design: Practitioner article drawing on the authors’ network consulting and research; illustrative cases.
strengths: Translates social network analysis into a usable managerial diagnostic; clear distinction among types of ties.
limitations: Case illustrations rather than systematic evidence; network surveys raise confidentiality and ethical concerns that the article treats briefly.
generalizability: Applies to any organization with interdependent work; the network types are general.
relevance: The practical bridge from network theory to the Influence Map you will build this week.

title: A Behavioral Theory of the Firm
publication: Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall (Prentice-Hall Behavioral Sciences in Business Series); second edition Blackwell, 1992
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, publisher (Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J.), 1963 date and series matched in library catalog records (catalog.lib.msu.edu, tuklas.up.edu.ph) and a 1964 review in the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science (cambridge.org); 1992 second edition reported.

summary: Cyert and March replace the profit-maximizing firm of economic theory with a firm that is a coalition of participants whose goals conflict and are negotiated. Goals emerge from bargaining, are stated as aspiration levels, are attended to sequentially, and are held together by side payments and organizational slack; firms search for solutions when performance falls below aspirations and settle for satisfactory rather than optimal outcomes.
arguments: The firm is a coalition of individuals and groups, not a single decision maker with one goal.
Organizational goals are the outcome of bargaining among coalition members and are revised by experience.
Conflict is never fully resolved; it is managed by attending to goals one at a time and by slack resources.
Firms satisfice and search locally, prompted by problems.
design: Theoretical book with case studies and computer models of firm decision making.
strengths: Founding text of the behavioral theory of organizations; makes politics a normal feature of organizational decision making rather than a pathology.
limitations: Abstract about the mechanics of coalition formation; empirical support comes mainly from later research rather than the book itself.
generalizability: High: the coalition view fits public agencies, professional service firms and sports organizations as well as industrial firms.
relevance: Any change you propose alters a negotiated settlement among coalition members; this book explains why that settlement exists.

title: The Iron Cage Revisited: Institutional Isomorphism and Collective Rationality in Organizational Fields
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 48, issue 2, pages 147–160 and DOI 10.2307/2095101 matched in a BibSonomy record, a ScienceGate record and Walter W. Powell’s Wikipedia bibliography.

summary: DiMaggio and Powell ask why organizations in the same field become so similar. They argue that once a field is established, organizations converge not mainly because similarity is efficient but through institutional isomorphism: coercive pressure from those they depend on and from the state, mimetic copying of organizations seen as successful when uncertainty is high, and normative pressure from professions and their training. Similarity confers legitimacy.
arguments: Organizational fields become homogeneous over time through institutional isomorphism.
Coercive isomorphism stems from dependence and political influence; mimetic isomorphism from uncertainty; normative isomorphism from professionalization.
Practices may be adopted for legitimacy whether or not they improve efficiency.
The paper offers testable hypotheses about which organizations and fields will change fastest.
design: Theoretical article with formal hypotheses; tested by a large later literature on the diffusion of practices.
strengths: Foundational to neo-institutional theory; explains why “everyone is doing it” is a powerful force independent of results.
limitations: Tends to overpredict sameness and underplay agency; isomorphic mechanisms are hard to separate empirically from rational learning.
contested: Debate continues on how to distinguish legitimacy-driven adoption from efficiency-driven adoption; resource dependence (R-pfeffer-1978-external) offers a competing explanation of conformity.
generalizability: High for public agencies, hospitals, universities, professional services and sports leagues, where professions and peer comparison are strong.
relevance: Helps you ask whether a proposed change is being adopted because it works or because peers have it — and how to use legitimacy honestly.

title: TVA and the Grass Roots: A Study in the Sociology of Formal Organization
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (University of California Press, Berkeley) and 1949 date matched in a 1949 American Political Science Review book-review record (econpapers.repec.org) and Wikipedia’s entry on Selznick; later editions (1980; 2010 reissue) reported. The publisher’s own page did not appear in results, so the review record is linked. Details of the argument were confirmed only at a general level (co-optation of local elites).

summary: Selznick’s study of the Tennessee Valley Authority examines how a federal agency committed to “grass-roots” democratic administration worked through established local institutions and elites. He develops the concept of co-optation — absorbing outside elements into an organization’s leadership or policy-making to avert threats to its stability — and shows how informal co-optation can shift an organization’s actual commitments away from its stated goals.
arguments: Co-optation is a mechanism for gaining support or neutralizing threat by bringing outsiders into the organization’s decision structure.
Formal co-optation shares the appearance of power; informal co-optation shares its substance with powerful local interests.
Co-opted interests can redirect an organization’s programs, so the price of support can be drift from the original mission.
Formal organizations develop informal structures and commitments that constrain leaders.
design: Historical-institutional case study of a single federal agency.
strengths: Rich case analysis; founding text for the “old” institutionalism and for the study of co-optation; directly relevant to public administration.
limitations: Single case; interpretive analysis; the agency’s history is specific to its era.
generalizability: The mechanism of co-optation generalizes well to any organization that buys support by sharing control; the specific findings are historical.
relevance: Every coalition strategy that gives a resister a seat at the table has the trade-off Selznick documented.

title: Social Influence: Compliance and Conformity

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 55, pages 591–621 and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 14744228) and citedrive.com.

summary: A review of compliance and conformity research published mainly between 1997 and 2002. Cialdini and Goldstein organize the literature around the goals that make people susceptible to influence — the desire to be accurate, to affiliate with others, and to maintain a positive self-concept — and argue that influence often operates subtly and outside awareness. The review covers the classic compliance principles, including reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity.
arguments: Compliance and conformity serve three broad goals: accuracy, affiliation and a positive self-concept.
Classic compliance principles can be understood as shortcuts toward those goals.
Influence often works through subtle, indirect processes outside awareness.
Norms — descriptive (what people do) and injunctive (what people approve) — are powerful influences on behavior.
design: Narrative review of the social influence literature.
strengths: Authoritative synthesis by the field’s best-known researcher; theoretical organization rather than a list of tricks.
limitations: Narrative, not meta-analytic; published before the replication crisis reshaped social psychology, so effect sizes of individual studies were not re-examined.
contested: Several individual findings in the influence literature have shown smaller or inconsistent effects in later replications; others, such as the door-in-the-face technique, replicated well (R-genschow-2021-does).
generalizability: The principles are general; the size of any technique’s effect in an organizational, repeated-relationship setting is uncertain.
relevance: Teaches the mechanisms behind persuasion so you can recognize them — when you use them and when they are used on you.

title: Does Social Psychology Persist over Half a Century? A Direct Replication of Cialdini et al.’s (1975) Classic Door-in-the-Face Technique
publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 120(2)
license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, journal, volume 120, issue 2 and DOI 10.1037/pspa0000261 matched on fis.leuphana.de, research.tilburguniversity.edu, zendy.io and the FORRT FLoRA replication atlas; first authors confirmed on kups.ub.uni-koeln.de. The full author list and page numbers were not confirmed, so only confirmed authors are listed. Some listings give 2020 (online-first).

summary: The authors directly replicated Cialdini and colleagues’ 1975 door-in-the-face study, in which a large initial request that is refused increases compliance with a smaller follow-up request. Running the study on a German university campus with 410 people approached by confederates, they found compliance rates similar to the original’s, and results consistent with the reciprocal-concessions explanation. The authors caution that this is one replication of one finding.
arguments: A classic compliance technique replicated in a different country, decades later.
The results support reciprocity norms (reciprocal concessions) as the mechanism.
Older social psychology findings have rarely been the target of direct replication.
design: Direct replication with confederates approaching people on a university campus; 410 participants.
strengths: Direct, preregistered-style replication of a field finding in a new culture; tests the theoretical mechanism, not only the effect.
limitations: One replication of one technique; student-campus setting with one-off requests by strangers, unlike repeated relationships at work.
contested: A positive data point in a mixed replication picture for the influence literature reviewed in R-cialdini-2004-social.
generalizability: Supports the existence of reciprocity-based concession effects; their size between colleagues who will deal with each other again is unknown.
relevance: Shows what a well-replicated influence finding looks like, so you can weigh the rest of the persuasion literature accordingly.

title: Consequences of Influence Tactics Used with Subordinates, Peers, and the Boss
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 77, issue 4, pages 525–535 and DOI matched on Cornell University’s eCommons repository (which hosts a PDF) and scilit.com; some reference lists render the title with “superiors” in place of “the boss”.

summary: Yukl and Tracey examined how the influence tactics managers use relate to the task commitment of the people they try to influence — subordinates, peers and bosses — and to ratings of the managers’ effectiveness. Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation were the tactics most associated with commitment; pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics were the least effective. Ingratiation and exchange were moderately effective with subordinates and peers but not with superiors.
arguments: Influence tactics differ in how likely they are to produce commitment rather than compliance or resistance.
Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation are most associated with commitment.
Pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics are least associated with commitment.
The direction of influence matters: some tactics work downward or laterally but not upward.
design: Field questionnaire study in which targets (subordinates, peers, bosses) described managers’ influence behavior and their own commitment; correlational.
strengths: Uses target reports rather than only agents’ self-reports; covers all three directions of influence; built on a validated taxonomy of tactics.
limitations: Cross-sectional and correlational; tactic choice is endogenous (people use pressure when they already expect resistance); common-method concerns.
generalizability: Reasonable for Western organizational settings; tactic effectiveness may differ across cultures and relationships.
relevance: Evidence-based guidance on influencing your peers and your boss, not only your staff.

title: Selling Issues to Top Management
license: © Academy of Management. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 18, issue 3 (July 1993), pages 397–428 and DOI 10.5465/AMR.1993.9309035145 matched on bibbase.org and searchworks; JSTOR identifier 10.2307/258903 also reported.

summary: Dutton and Ashford argue that middle managers shape what top management pays attention to by “selling” issues — calling attention to trends, events and problems and framing them. They develop a framework drawing on three perspectives: issue selling as upward influence, as claiming behavior (asserting that an issue deserves attention), and as impression management, since sellers risk their image. The framework explains when managers will try to sell an issue and how the way they package it and the process they use affects success.
arguments: Top management’s agenda is shaped from below by the issues middle managers choose to raise.
Whether managers try to sell an issue depends on perceived chances of success and on image risk.
Success depends on how an issue is packaged (framing, bundling) and on the selling process (timing, channels, involvement of others).
Issue selling is a political act and an impression-management act at once.
design: Theoretical framework with propositions; later tested in field studies by the authors and colleagues.
strengths: Puts middle managers at the center of strategic change; generated a substantial empirical literature.
limitations: Propositions rather than tests; draws on U.S. corporate settings.
generalizability: Applies to anyone who needs senior attention for an issue they do not own — in firms, agencies, hospitals or sports organizations.
relevance: The core theory of managing upward when you want leaders to care about your issue.
